## Why environments exist: the "works on my machine" problem

Your operating system ships with a Python (the **system interpreter**), and it's tempting to just
`pip install` everything into it. Don't. Two projects will eventually disagree: one needs
`numpy 1.26`, the other `numpy 2.1`; one wants Python 3.11, the other 3.12. A single shared
interpreter can't satisfy both, and "fixing" one project silently breaks another. The classic
symptom is the bug that only reproduces on *your* laptop — and the equally classic non-fix, "well,
it works on my machine."

A **virtual environment** solves this by giving each project its *own* isolated interpreter and its
*own* `site-packages` directory. Activating it puts that project's Python first on your `PATH`, so
`import numpy` resolves to *this project's* numpy and nobody else's.

::: {.callout-tip}
The mental model: a virtual environment is a sandboxed copy of "Python + the packages this one
project needs." Throw it away and recreate it at will — it's derived, not precious.
:::

Isolation gets you "doesn't clash with other projects." The second half of reproducibility is
**pinning**: recording the *exact* version of every package (and every package *those* depend on)
so a fresh machine installs the identical set. Why bother being exact? Because risk compounds. If
each of your `n` dependencies has even a small independent probability $p_i$ of resolving to a
subtly different, breaking version when left unpinned, the chance the whole environment reproduces
cleanly is

$$
P_\text{reproduce} = \prod_{i=1}^{n} (1 - p_i).
$$

With 50 loosely-specified dependencies at just 1% risk each, that's $0.99^{50} \approx 0.61$ — a
roughly **40% chance something drifts**. The fix is a **lockfile**: pin everything, and $p_i \to 0$.

## The modern toolchain: `uv`

[`uv`](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/) is a fast, all-in-one Python project manager (from Astral, the
Ruff folks). It handles the interpreter, the virtual environment, dependency resolution, and the
lockfile — replacing a pile of older tools with one. **This course standardizes on it**, and this
very website is built with it.

The workflow is a short pipeline. You declare what you *want* in `pyproject.toml`; `uv` computes
the exact, reproducible graph into `uv.lock`; `uv sync` materializes that into a `.venv`; and
`uv run` executes your code inside it.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["<b>pyproject.toml</b><br/>declared deps<br/>(numpy, …)"] -->|uv lock| B["<b>uv.lock</b><br/>exact pinned graph"]
  B -->|uv sync| C["<b>.venv</b><br/>isolated interpreter<br/>+ packages"]
  C -->|uv run| D["your code ·<br/>Jupyter · Quarto"]
```

In practice you rarely run `uv lock` by hand — `uv add` and `uv run` keep the lockfile and `.venv`
current for you. A typical first session:

```bash
uv init my-project          # scaffold pyproject.toml
cd my-project
uv add numpy pandas         # add deps; updates pyproject.toml + uv.lock + .venv
uv run python script.py     # run inside the project's env (auto-syncs first)
```

Cloning an existing project (like this repo) is just two steps — exactly what its `CLAUDE.md`
documents:

```bash
uv sync                     # recreate .venv from pyproject.toml / uv.lock
uv run quarto preview       # run a command inside that env
```

Because `uv.lock` is committed to git, a teammate (or CI, or you in six months) runs `uv sync` and
gets the **byte-identical** dependency set. That's the reproducibility guarantee from the previous
section, made concrete.

::: {.callout-note title="Where conda and pip+venv fit"}
- **`pip` + `venv`** — the standard-library baseline (`python -m venv .venv && pip install …`). It
  works everywhere and is worth understanding, but it's slower and doesn't produce a lockfile by
  itself. Think of `uv` as a faster, batteries-included superset.
- **conda / mamba** — shines when you need **non-Python** system libraries (CUDA toolkits, MKL,
  GDAL, compilers) bundled as prebuilt binaries, common in scientific and some GPU stacks. If your
  stack is pure-Python, `uv` is simpler and faster; reach for conda when native dependencies fight you.
:::

## Running code: Jupyter & VS Code

You'll spend most of this course in two places: **Jupyter notebooks** (for exploratory,
cell-by-cell work — every tutorial ships a paired notebook) and **VS Code** (for editing files and
projects). The concept that ties them to your environment is the **kernel**.

A notebook is just cells of code, prose, and saved output. When you run a cell, the code executes
in a separate Python process called the **kernel**. The single most common Jupyter confusion is a
notebook whose kernel is some *other* Python than your project's — so `import numpy` fails even
though you "definitely installed it." The rule: **point the kernel at your project's `.venv`.**

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  NB["Notebook<br/>(.ipynb cells)"] -->|sends code to| K["Kernel<br/>(Python process)"]
  K -.->|should be| V[".venv<br/>(this project's interpreter)"]
```

- **Jupyter:** `uv run jupyter lab` launches Jupyter *using the project venv*, so the default kernel
  is already the right one.
- **VS Code:** install the Python + Jupyter extensions, open the project folder, then use the
  interpreter / kernel picker (bottom-right, or the "Select Kernel" button on a notebook) to choose
  the `.venv` interpreter. VS Code can then run notebooks and scripts against it directly.

## Worked example: a self-test script

The best way to confirm an environment is real is to *ask Python about itself*. This little report
runs at build time — no GPU, no network — and is the kind of smoke test worth running right after
`uv sync`:

```{python}
import sys
import platform

print("Python version :", platform.python_version())
print("Platform       :", platform.system(), platform.machine())

# A trivial computation that must succeed if the interpreter works at all.
assert sum(range(10)) == 45
print("Sanity check   : OK")
```

The single most useful field, though, is **`sys.executable`** — the absolute path of the
interpreter running this code. It's the giveaway for *which* Python you're actually on:

```python
>>> import sys; sys.executable
'/home/user/ai-engineer/.venv/bin/python3'   # ← should sit inside your project's .venv
```

It should point *inside* your project's `.venv`, not at the system Python (e.g.
`/usr/bin/python3`). If it doesn't, your shell — or your notebook kernel — isn't using the
environment you think it is.

## Key takeaways

- A **virtual environment** isolates each project's interpreter and packages, killing cross-project
  version clashes and the "works on my machine" bug.
- Reproducibility = isolation **+ pinning**; risk compounds across dependencies, so a committed
  **lockfile** (`uv.lock`) is what makes a fresh `uv sync` reproduce your setup exactly.
- **`uv` is the daily driver**: `uv add` to change deps, `uv run` to execute inside the env. Use
  conda when you need native/system binaries; pip+venv is the stdlib baseline underneath it all.
- A Jupyter **kernel** is just a Python process — point it at your project `.venv`, and check
  `sys.executable` when imports mysteriously fail.

## Check your understanding

**1.** What exactly does a virtual environment isolate, and what concrete problem does that isolation
solve?

::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"}
It isolates the **interpreter** and the **`site-packages`** (installed packages) for one project.
That lets two projects depend on conflicting versions (e.g. `numpy 1.26` vs `2.1`) without
interfering, which prevents the "installing for project A broke project B / it only works on my
machine" class of bug.
:::

**2.** What's the difference between `pyproject.toml` and `uv.lock`, and which one actually guarantees
that two machines get the same packages?

::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"}
`pyproject.toml` declares the dependencies you *want*, often with loose ranges (e.g. `numpy>=1.26`).
`uv.lock` records the **exact resolved version of every package and transitive dependency**. The
**lockfile** is what guarantees reproducibility — `uv sync` installs precisely what it pins, so a
fresh machine gets a byte-identical set.
:::

**3.** Why does an environment get *less* likely to reproduce cleanly as you add more loosely-pinned
dependencies?

::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"}
Each unpinned dependency carries an independent chance of resolving to a different, possibly
breaking version. Those chances multiply: $P_\text{reproduce} = \prod_i (1 - p_i)$. Even tiny
per-package risk compounds across dozens of packages (e.g. $0.99^{50} \approx 0.61$), so more
unpinned deps means a higher overall chance something drifts. Pinning via a lockfile drives each
$p_i$ toward zero.
:::

**4.** In Jupyter, what is a "kernel," and how should it relate to your project's virtual environment?

::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"}
A kernel is the separate **Python process** that actually executes a notebook's cells. It should be
the interpreter from your project's `.venv`, so that imports resolve to the packages you installed
for that project. A mismatched kernel is the usual cause of "I installed it but the import fails."
Launching with `uv run jupyter lab` (or selecting the `.venv` interpreter in VS Code) ensures the
right kernel.
:::

**5.** You need a package that bundles a CUDA toolkit and some compiled native libraries as prebuilt
binaries. Would you reach for `uv` or conda, and why?

::: {.callout-tip title="Show answer" collapse="true"}
**conda (or mamba).** Its strength is shipping **non-Python / system-level binaries** (CUDA, MKL,
compilers, GDAL) as prebuilt packages, which is awkward with pip/uv. For pure-Python stacks, `uv`
is simpler and faster — but when native dependencies fight you, conda is the right tool.
:::

## Coding tasks

Work these in the paired notebook — open it in Colab (no GPU needed for Day 2):

### Task 1 — Environment self-check

Write a function `env_report()` that prints the running Python version (use `sys.version_info`) and
the platform, and then **asserts** that Python is at least **3.10** (raise a clear error otherwise).
Call it to confirm your interpreter is the one you expect.

{{< colab notebooks/01-foundations/02-environment-setup.ipynb >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Show solution" collapse="true"}
```python
import sys
import platform

def env_report():
    v = sys.version_info
    print(f"Python  : {v.major}.{v.minor}.{v.micro}")
    print(f"Platform: {platform.system()} {platform.machine()}")
    assert v >= (3, 10), f"Need Python >= 3.10, got {v.major}.{v.minor}"
    print("Interpreter OK ✅")

env_report()
```
:::

### Task 2 — Confirm a package is installed and working

A real "does my env work?" test imports a third-party package and *uses* it. Write
`check_numpy()` that imports `numpy`, prints its version (`numpy.__version__`), builds the array
`[1, 2, 3]`, and asserts its sum equals `6`. If the import fails, print a helpful message telling the
reader to run `uv add numpy` (or `pip install numpy`).

{{< colab notebooks/01-foundations/02-environment-setup.ipynb >}}

::: {.callout-tip title="Show solution" collapse="true"}
```python
def check_numpy():
    try:
        import numpy as np
    except ImportError:
        print("numpy is not installed — run `uv add numpy` (or `pip install numpy`).")
        return
    print(f"numpy   : {np.__version__}")
    a = np.array([1, 2, 3])
    assert a.sum() == 6
    print("numpy works ✅")

check_numpy()
```
:::
